ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Social psychological research has identified two expressions of hypodescent in humans: a classification bias, in which White participants are more likely to classify a biracial face as Black than as White (29, 33), and a representation bias, whereby participants' mental image of a Black-White biracial face is more similar to a Black than White face (34, 35).

> Sampling was based on FairFace image labels, annotated by Amazon Mechanical Turk workers who, in 2020, were USbased and primarily White (57).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .05", Text = "Means within a row that do not share a common subscript differ significantly at p < .05 (Tukey HSD). ***p < .001."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .102", Sentence = "However, this gendered-race pattern was not significantly moderated by dataset imbalance (three-way interaction: F(3, 60) = 2.16, p = .102)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. info.title: Data Diversity and Algorithmic Bias: Do Racially-Imbalanced Training Data Produce Human-Like Bias in Face Classification?
keywords: Gender Dataset Diversity & Face Classification AI 2

text.text: Can a lack of racial diversity in training data produce human-like forms of AI face classification bias?

We examined the causal effect of racially-imbalanced training data on face classification model disparities and whether these disparities resemble three well-documented human biases-the cross-race effect, hypodescent, and the gendered-race effect.
We further examined whether balanced training data mitigate these disparities.

In three experiments, we trained deep Vision Transformer models for face classification on 16,000 face images, experimentally manipulating racial composition while holding other dataset features and training procedures constant.
Study 1 showed that models trained on low-diversity (majority-White) datasets classified White faces more accurately than Black, East Asian, and Indian faces, resembling the human cross-race effect.

In Study 2, using parametrically-morphed Black-White biracial face images to estimate race-classification thresholds, lower-diversity models required more Black than White content to reach this threshold, yet represented biracial faces with more Black content.

Lastly, Study 3 revealed a gendered-race effect: regardless of training set imbalance, models classified Black men more accurately than Black women, but East Asian women more accurately than East Asian men.
The use of racially-balanced training data nearly eliminated disparities in monoracial classification, reduced bias in biracial classification, but it did not alter the gendered-race effect.
These findings show that training data composition causally shapes algorithmic performance in ways that both mimic and diverge from human biases.
We discuss implications for AI-based discrimination and both the promise and limitations of data balancing as a strategy to mitigate algorithmic bias.

Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to classify socially meaningful human categories from facial images, with applications ranging from identity verification and surveillance to policing, security, and marketing (1) (2) (3)).

text.text: Yet face classification systems have been found to exhibit systematic racial disparities, including lower accuracy for women and people with darker skin tones (4, 5).
text.formatted: Yet face classification systems have been found to exhibit systematic racial disparities, including lower accuracy for women and people with darker skin tones <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5)</ref>.

text.text: Such disparities can be especially harmful when AI outputs inform high-stakes decisions, such as in policing (6) (7) (8), and particularly when they align with existing patterns of human racial bias (9, 10).
text.formatted: Such disparities can be especially harmful when AI outputs inform high-stakes decisions, such as in policing <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>, and particularly when they align with existing patterns of human racial bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10)</ref>.

text.text: To date, however, the causal impact of training data imbalance on racial disparities in face classification, and their resemblance to human social perception, has not been investigated.

Here, we experimentally tested whether racial imbalances in training data produce racial disparities in face classification model performance and, if so, whether these disparities mimic well-known human biases in face categorization.

Demographic characteristics of faces-including race and gender-are known to influence the performance of AI systems for face detection, recognition, and classification, producing systematic disparities in model output (11) (12) (13) (14) (15).
text.formatted: Demographic characteristics of faces-including race and gender-are known to influence the performance of AI systems for face detection, recognition, and classification, producing systematic disparities in model output <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>.

text.text: These disparities have been attributed, in part, to racial imbalances in the datasets used to train classification models (4, 5, (16) (17) (18) (19).
text.formatted: These disparities have been attributed, in part, to racial imbalances in the datasets used to train classification models <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.text: For example, many existing benchmark datasets (e.g., LFW+, IJB-A, Adience, CelebA) have been reported to contain high proportions of White faces (e.g., 80% or more) and uneven representations of other racial/ethnic groups, in addition to imbalances on other demographic characteristics (4, 5, 20, 21).
text.formatted: For example, many existing benchmark datasets (e.g., LFW+, IJB-A, Adience, CelebA) have been reported to contain high proportions of White faces (e.g., 80% or more) and uneven representations of other racial/ethnic groups, in addition to imbalances on other demographic characteristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this account, models trained on existing majority-White datasets have been found to produce racial disparities in gender classification-that is, lower accuracy for people of color, particularly for women (4, 5).
text.formatted: Consistent with this account, models trained on existing majority-White datasets have been found to produce racial disparities in gender classification-that is, lower accuracy for people of color, particularly for women <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, when models were trained on more racially-balanced datasets, these disparities were reduced.

However, while informative, the existing evidence is limited because it has not established whether these disparities arise from racial composition specifically or from correlated properties of the datasets being compared.

This is because the datasets used in prior work differ on dimensions besides race or ethnicity, such as image quality, sample size, annotation procedures, sampling context, preprocessing, and other demographic characteristics (e.g., age).
As a result, differences associated with such datasets cannot be causally attributed to racial imbalance alone.
Rather, a causal attribution would require an experimental approach, in which racial balance is manipulated while other dataset features are held constant.
Furthermore, most studies on the effects of dataset imbalance have, to date, focused on gender classification (4, 5).
text.formatted: Furthermore, most studies on the effects of dataset imbalance have, to date, focused on gender classification <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5)</ref>.

text.text: Although some research has observed performance decrements in race classification for minority faces trained on White-dominant data (22), the effects of dataset imbalance on race classification-and whether these effects resemble human patterns of racial bias-have not been systematically investigated.
text.formatted: Although some research has observed performance decrements in race classification for minority faces trained on White-dominant data <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref>, the effects of dataset imbalance on race classification-and whether these effects resemble human patterns of racial bias-have not been systematically investigated.

text.text: If racially imbalanced training data produce disparities in model performance, to what extent do these disparities resemble common human biases in race perception?
Psychology research on human face categorization has identified three well-documented patterns of racial bias: the cross-race effect, perceptual hypodescent, and the gendered-race effect.
Each captures a distinct pattern of categorization and therefore provides a social psychological benchmark for evaluating the effects of training data composition on AI face classification.
Cross-race effect.

The cross-race effect (or other-race effect) describes the tendency for people to recognize ingroup faces more accurately than outgroup faces (23, 24)-an effect attributed to both perceptual expertise and preferences for ingroup members (25, 26).
text.formatted: The cross-race effect (or other-race effect) describes the tendency for people to recognize ingroup faces more accurately than outgroup faces <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24)</ref>-an effect attributed to both perceptual expertise and preferences for ingroup members <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26)</ref>.

text.text: In AI systems, a cross-race pattern has been observed for facial recognition: models developed in Western countries performed more accurately for White faces than East Asian faces, whereas the opposite pattern was found for models developed in East Asian countries (27).

text.text: In the context of race classification, existing studies suggest a pattern analogous to the cross-race effect (22), such that the use of majority-White training data would lead models to classify White faces more accurately than faces from underrepresented racial groups.

text.text: Human racial categorization also exhibits a pattern of hypodescent: the tendency to categorize people of mixed racial ancestry according to their lower-status racial group (28).

text.text: For example, White Americans tend to perceive Black-White biracial faces as Black rather than White (29-31)-a pattern linked to intergroup motives for power and resources (32, 33).

text.text: Social psychological research has identified two expressions of hypodescent in humans: a classification bias, in which White participants are more likely to classify a biracial face as Black than as White (29, 33), and a representation bias, whereby participants' mental image of a Black-White biracial face is more similar to a Black than White face (34, 35).

text.text: In the context of AI, research using a visual semantic model (Contrastive Language Image Pretraining; CLIP) to assign racial labels to face images found that biracial faces tended to be labeled according to their lower-status identity (36).

text.text: In terms of face classification, a computational analogue would be a systematic classification of biracial faces as belonging to the lower-status racial group.
Testing this possibility requires moving beyond monoracial classification to the classification of biracial faces that vary systematically in racial composition.
Race also shapes human gender categorization through the genderedrace effect-an intersectional expression of racial stereotypes in gender perception (37).
text.formatted: Race also shapes human gender categorization through the genderedrace effect-an intersectional expression of racial stereotypes in gender perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(37)</ref>.

text.text: For example, consistent with US stereotypes of Black people as aggressive and dominant and East Asian people as docile and submissive (38, 39), White American perceivers are more likely to categorize gender-ambiguous Black faces as male and gender-ambiguous East Asian faces as female (37, 40).

text.text: In AI face classification, a corresponding pattern would be reflected in an interaction between race and gender in gender classification accuracy: specifically, greater accuracy for Black men than Black women, but greater accuracy for Asian women than Asian men.
This pattern would expand on previously-reported performance decrements for women of color (4) to place it within a broader pattern of racial stereotype effects on gender classification.

Together, these three bias benchmarks from psychological research capture distinct dimensions of social categorization: differences in monoracial classification accuracy across racial groups, the categorization of biracial identities, and interactive effects of race and gender on gender classification.

Although AI classification systems might not reproduce these human biases exactly, an assessment of where their performance mimics or diverges from patterns of human social perception can help to identify specific disparity patterns and inform their potential influence on human users.

The present research tested whether racial composition in training data causally shapes face classification performance and whether the resulting disparities converge with or diverge from established patterns of human social bias.

In each of three studies, we manipulated the racial composition of the training data for White faces relative to Black, East Asian, and Indian faces, using 27,040 randomly-drawn images and corresponding labels from FairFace (5).

text.text: From this sample, we created four separate training datasets, each comprising 16,000 images, which varied systematically in racial composition while holding gender balance and proportion of minority faces constant within each condition (Figure 1).
text.formatted: From this sample, we created four separate training datasets, each comprising 16,000 images, which varied systematically in racial composition while holding gender balance and proportion of minority faces constant within each condition (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: This design allowed us to compare an extreme White-dominance condition (94% White)-designed to approximate publicly-available datasets shown previously to produce biased classification (4, 5)-to conditions with progressively increasing racial balance (75%, 50%, and 25% White, i.e., fully-balanced).

To build classification models, we used a Vision Transformer (ViT) pretrained on ImageNet-21k and fine-tuned it end-to-end on each manipulated training dataset, replacing the final classification layer with a task-specific linear head predicting either race (Studies 1-2) or gender (Study 3).
To account for variability due to sampling and stochastic optimization, each condition was trained with five independent random seeds.

For each seed, a new training dataset was generated according to the condition-specific demographic constraints (balanced versus imbalanced race distributions), ensuring that differences between conditions reflected controlled changes in data composition rather than idiosyncrasies of individual images.

All models were evaluated on a balanced held-out test set containing 6,024 face images with equal numbers of images for each Race × Gender combination, such that any differences in accuracy could not be attributed to subgroup frequencies in the test data (see Methods).

In Study 1, we tested the effect of dataset diversity on race classification accuracy (proportion of correct race predictions out of all race predictions), using the experimental manipulation and procedures for model training and evaluation described above.

A seed-blocked factorial ANOVA produced significant main effects of both race, F(3, 60) = 109.67, p < .001, and training balance condition, F(3, 60) = 62.63, p < .001, indicating higher overall accuracy for White faces and for models trained on balanced datasets.

text.text: However, these effects were qualified by the Condition × Race interaction, F(9, 60) = 21.17, p < .001 (Figure 2), indicating that race classification disparities depended on dataset balance.

text.text: The analyses revealed a large classification accuracy disparity in the extreme imbalance condition, which incrementally decreased as datasets became more balanced.
In the fullybalanced condition, this disparity was fully mitigated among White, Black, and East Asian faces, with a relatively small disparity remaining for Indian faces.
Notably, classification accuracy was consistently lowest for Indian faces, potentially suggesting greater variability in the images or annotator labels, among other possible factors.
In addition to reducing mean classification accuracy for underrepresented racial groups, training data imbalance was associated with greater variability across independently trained models.
In the balanced condition, variability was small and comparable across racial groups (White: SD = .011; Black: SD = .007; East Asian: SD = .008; Indian: SD = .011).
Under extreme White dominance, variability remained low for White faces (SD = .005) but increased substantially for Black (SD = .067), East Asian (SD = .084), and Indian faces (SD = .096).
The intermediate conditions showed a graded pattern: SDs for underrepresented groups ranged from .013 to .018 under moderate White dominance and from .016 to .034 under strong White dominance.
This greater variability may have reflected both the smaller number of available training images and variability in the images randomly selected for each seed.
This pattern suggests an effect of imbalance on model stability, in addition to classification accuracy, particularly when imbalance creates categories with relatively scarce data.
These results provide experimental evidence that training data composition causally shapes racial disparities in face classification.
Models trained on extreme White-dominant datasets classified White faces more accurately than faces from underrepresented racial groups, analogous to the human cross-race effect.
These disparities decreased as training datasets became more racially balanced and were largely eliminated.

text.text: In Study 2, we asked whether dataset diversity affects a model's classification of biracial facesthat is, whether racial imbalance alters the threshold for race classification under conditions of ambiguity.
To this end, we created a controlled set of biracial test images to submit to models trained in Study 1.

Test faces (N = 4,180, see Method) were morphs of real Black and White faces, representing 380 unique spectra along which faces varied parametrically in their proportion of Black-White composition on an 11-point continuum, from 0% Black (100% White) to 100% Black (0% White) (Figure 3).

Test images from each morph spectrum were submitted independently to each of the four models created in Study 1, representing the four conditions of training dataset imbalance.

For each condition, across test images, classification probabilities for Black and White categories were obtained and used to compute each model's point of subjective equality (PSE)-the point along the morph spectrum at which a face is equally likely to be classified as Black or White.

A PSE of 0.50 corresponds to an unbiased threshold at the objective midpoint of the continuum (morph faces with 50% White and 50% Black content are classified as equally likely to be Black versus White).

Values below 0.50 indicate that faces containing less than 50% Black content (i.e., have greater White content than Black content) are equally likely to be classified as Black than as White-a pattern consistent with the perceptual hypodescent effect seen in humans (33, 41).

By contrast, values above 0.50 indicate that faces containing more than 50% Black content (i.e., have greater Black content than White content) are equally likely to be classified as White than as Black-a pattern opposite to the human hypodescent bias.
To estimate condition-level PSEs, morph spectra were resampled with replacement over 1,000 bootstrap iterations.
A PSE was recalculated for each resampled dataset.
We report the mean of these bootstrap PSE estimates and percentile-based 95% confidence intervals, which reflect variation across morph spectra while keeping the trained models fixed.
Results indicated that race-classification thresholds differed by training set imbalance.
A repeated-measures ANOVA of per-spectrum PSE scores revealed a significant main effect of training balance condition, F(3, 1137) = 1102.29, p < .001.

text.text: However, the resulting pattern diverged from human hypodescent: in the extreme White-dominance condition , the mean PSE was .77 (95% CI [.76,.78])-a threshold substantially above 50%-indicating that a face containing up to 77% Black content would have an equal chance of being classified as either Black or White.

The PSE was significantly lower in the strong White-dominance condition (M=.66, 95% CI [.66,.67]), the moderate White-dominance condition (M=.69, 95% CI [.68,.69]), and the balanced condition (M=.64, 95% CI [.63,.65]).
Although the balanced model's threshold was closer to .50 than other conditions, it was nonetheless significantly above the point of compositional parity.

These results demonstrate that models trained on datasets with greater White dominance can result in a Black-White race classification threshold that requires greater Black than White racial composition.

This pattern contrasts with the hypodescent classification effect observed in humans and suggests that AI systems would be more likely to identify biracial faces as Black than as White-a pattern of bias that may have different implications for discrimination than in humans.
It is notable, however, that hypodescent in humans is also expressed in mental representations of biracial faces as being more Black than White (34, 35).

To explore this possibility, we selected the 50 images closest to the classification boundary (i.e., identified as 50:50 biracial) separately for the extreme White-dominance and balanced models.

text.text: In summary, Study 2 shows that training data composition systematically shifts a model's biracial classification threshold.

All four conditions yielded PSEs substantially above .5, indicating a classification boundary requiring greater Black than White content-a pattern that contrasts with human hypodescent effects in race categorization.
However, this threshold was higher for models trained on imbalanced than balanced datasets.

Additionally, as a consequence of these model threshold differences, White-dominant models appeared to represent biracial faces with greater Black than White content than the balanced model-a pattern that converges with hypodescent in humans' mental representations of biracial faces.

In Study 3, we asked whether a racial imbalance in training data affects gender classificationthat is, whether models exhibit a gendered-race effect, such that gender classification performance varies by race in a manner consistent with racial stereotypes.
The same data and model architecture were used as in Study 1, except that we trained classification models to predict binary gender (female, male).

A factorial ANOVA with condition, race, and gender as fixed factors, and seed included as a blocking factor, produced significant main effects of condition, F(3, 124) = 7.96, p < .001, race, F(3, 124) = 355.98, p < .001, and gender, F(1, 124) = 7.89, p = .006 (Table S1 in SI).

text.text: Of these, the main effect of condition indicated that overall gender accuracy improved as models became more balanced.
Importantly, these main effects were qualified by a significant Race × Gender interaction, F(3, 124) = 66.02, p < .001, such that gender classification performance varied as a function of race.

This analysis revealed a significant Race × Gender interaction, F(1, 60) = 119.25, p < .001.

text.text: Simple-effect analyses indicated the gendered-race pattern: for Black faces, males (M = .911, SD = .013) were classified more accurately than females (M = .869, SD = .009), t(60) = 5.31, p < .001, whereas the reverse was found for East Asian faces, such that females (M = .944, SD = .009) were classified more accurately than males (M = .921, SD = .009), t(60) = 2.91, p = .005.

text.text: However, this gendered-race pattern was not significantly moderated by dataset imbalance (three-way interaction: F(3, 60) = 2.16, p = .102).
Study 3 therefore revealed a prominent gendered-race effect across all face classification models.

Furthermore, gender classification models did not just perform worse for underrepresented racial groups or for a specific intersectional category (e.g., Black women); rather, gender classification performance showed a pattern of bias consistent with US racial stereotypes that associate Black people with more masculine traits and East Asian people with more feminine traits.
Unlike the race classification effects in Studies 1 and 2, the use of raciallybalanced training data did not significantly reduce the gendered-race effect in face classification performance.
We investigated whether racial composition in AI training data shapes face classification patterns and whether such patterns resemble known human biases in social categorization.

By manipulating dataset racial balance while controlling for image source, training set size, gender balance, and model parameters, we examined computational analogues of three welldocumented patterns of human racial bias in face categorization-the cross-race, hypodescent, and gendered-race effects (42).

text.text: We found that training data composition can causally alter the structure of classification behavior, producing patterns that both converge and diverge with common biases in human social perception.

Study 1 showed that models trained on datasets with disproportionately White faces, like many publicly-available datasets, performed much more accurately for White faces than Black, East Asian, and Indian faces-a pattern akin to the human cross-race effect.
However, these disparities decreased progressively with greater racial balance and were largely eliminated in the fully-balanced condition.
These results provide experimental evidence that racial imbalances in training data can causally produce disparities in race classification.
Study 2 extended this approach to the classification of racially ambiguous faces.
Dataset imbalance again impacted performance, shifting the decision boundary for racial classification, but in a direction opposite to the bias observed in White participants.

That is, whereas human perceivers tend to classify Black-White biracial faces as Black, the models here tended to classify biracial faces as White-an effect that was strongest for the extreme White-dominant model.

However, as a consequence of these classification thresholds, imbalanced models appeared to represent biracial faces as having greater Black content (i.e., appeared more Black) than the balanced model-a pattern mimicking a different human expression of hypodescent whereby mental representations of biracial faces are more Black than White (34, 35).

text.text: These findings suggest that depending on how an AI face classification system is used, its results could parallel or contrast with human hypodescent bias.
Study 3 examined the effect of racial imbalance on gender classification.

Across conditions, models more accurately classified the gender of Black male faces than Black female faces, and of East Asian female faces than East Asian male faces-a specific interaction pattern resembling the gendered-race effect in humans in which racial stereotypes influence gender categorization (37, 40).
text.formatted: Across conditions, models more accurately classified the gender of Black male faces than Black female faces, and of East Asian female faces than East Asian male faces-a specific interaction pattern resembling the gendered-race effect in humans in which racial stereotypes influence gender categorization <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40)</ref>.

text.text: This finding suggests that prior observations of diminished gender classification accuracy for Black women may reflect a broader intersectional pattern involving multiple racial groups (4).
Although racial balancing improved overall gender classification accuracy, it did not significantly alter the specific gendered-race pattern observed for Black and East Asian faces.

Thus, the origins of this pattern remain unclear, but may be due to annotator bias in the labeling of training images, systematic features of the images themselves, or other aspects of model training.
Together, these studies reveal both the value and limits of using human social cognition as a framework for understanding algorithmic bias.
The cross-race and gendered-race patterns in our models resembled established human biases, whereas the biracial classification thresholds diverged from human perceptual hypodescent.

These similarities and differences suggest that examining AI outputs through the lens of human psychology can reveal distinct forms of disparity that may be overlooked by aggregate measures of model accuracy.
At the same time, similarities between human and AI classification patterns should not be taken as evidence of shared underlying mechanisms.

Human racial categorization is shaped by factors such as perceptual experience, stereotypes, and intergroup motivation, whereas AI classification reflects statistical regularities in training data and the optimization processes used to fit model parameters.
These findings also raise questions about how algorithmic disparities might interact with human judgment.

Existing psychological research has demonstrated that people are more receptive to information that confirms their existing expectations and stereotypes, influencing consequential judgments such as eyewitness evaluations and assessments of job candidates (24, 43, 44).

text.text: Research on humans' use of AI finds similar patterns of confirmation bias (9, 45, 46).

text.text: Thus, if AI systems produce outputs that align with stereotypical perceptions and expectancies, users may be less likely to detect or correct for these biases.
Though not the aim of the present work, identifying the effect of these bias patterns on human decision making is an important next step toward determining its impact on AI-based discrimination.
Regarding bias mitigation, our studies suggest that balanced training data can reduce some forms of algorithmic bias but not others.
For AI systems designed for single-category race classification, as in Study 1, balanced race representation may effectively mitigate bias.

But when the relationship between racial composition of training data and the classification objective was less direct-such as when classifying mixed-race identities or gender in Studies 2 and 3-dataset balance did not eliminate disparities.

As such, additional approaches warrant investigation, including those that target model training procedures, such as efforts to prevent hidden correlations between social categories represented in training data, as well as psychology-based interventions, such as procedures to improve accuracy and reduce bias in human annotation (6, (47) (48) (49) (50).

text.text: Our findings highlight a broader risk of systems that impose rigid categorical identities on individuals.
Classifiers that assign people to a single race or gender can misclassify those who do not fit neatly into one category (51).
text.formatted: Classifiers that assign people to a single race or gender can misclassify those who do not fit neatly into one category <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(51)</ref>.

text.text: Such systems may also reproduce and reinforce the categorical frameworks through which social differences are constructed and reinforced, potentially contributing to discrimination and inequality (52).
text.formatted: Such systems may also reproduce and reinforce the categorical frameworks through which social differences are constructed and reinforced, potentially contributing to discrimination and inequality <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(52)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should therefore examine not only how to improve classification within existing frameworks, but also whether systems that accommodate multidimensional or uncertain identities can reduce the harms associated with rigid categorization.
Our conclusions should be interpreted in light of several limitations.
First, we examined Whitemajority training datasets, given the prevalence of White-dominant datasets and their relevance to racial disparities in AI.
However, bias-related effects may differ under other configurations of demographic imbalance.

Second, the gendered-race pattern we observed concerns Black and East Asian faces and their associated stereotypes in a US cultural context, yet different patterns may emerge in other cultural settings.

Third, while our experimental design isolated effects of training data composition within our model training pipeline, other factors-such as FairFace labels, ImageNet pretraining, image preprocessing, sampling procedures, and model architecture-could also affect classification outcomes.

Lastly, our design does not disentangle the effects of racial group proportions from the absolute number of minority-group images, because these features vary together as the composition of a fixedsize dataset changes.
Future research could manipulate these factors independently to identify their respective contributions.

More broadly, our findings illustrate the value of an integrated computational-psychological approach to algorithmic bias, treating AI systems as products of machine learning processes embedded in human social contexts (53) (54) (55).

Sampling was based on FairFace image labels, annotated by Amazon Mechanical Turk workers who, in 2020, were USbased and primarily White (57).

text.text: From this pool, we constructed four training datasets of 16,000 images each, comprising unique White-, Black-, East Asian-, and Indian-labeled faces across four conditions that varied in their proportion of White faces (94%, 75%, 50%, 25%), with equal proportions of the three non-White racial groups and balanced gender within race.
To include a sufficient number of images for each condition, East Asian and Southeast Asian categories were combined, and Middle Eastern, Latino, and "Other" were excluded.
This sample size (16,000) was chosen because it was the largest possible sample that permitted controlled manipulations of racial imbalance while preserving gender balance within race.
Vision Transformer (ViT-Base/16) models (58), pretrained on ImageNet-21k, were fine-tuned end-to-end on the manipulated training datasets.
The original classification layer was replaced with a newly initialized linear classification head predicting race (Studies 1 and 2) or gender (Study 3).

All images were converted to RGB and processed using the pretrained model's image processor, which resized images to 224 × 224 pixels and applied the corresponding rescaling and normalization procedures.
No data augmentation was used.

To account for variability due to data sampling and stochastic optimisation, five models were trained independently within each experimental condition, each using a separately sampled training dataset drawn from the FairFace training pool according to the conditionspecific demographic constraints.
Models were trained for up to 10 epochs using the AdamW optimizer, a learning rate of 6 × 10⁻⁵, a batch size of 64, and cross-entropy loss, with a cosine learning-rate schedule and 10% warmup.
The checkpoint achieving the highest macro-F1 score on the balanced validation set was retained for subsequent analyses.
Model training was conducted on the Snellius supercomputer using one NVIDIA A100 GPU, eight CPU cores, and 48 GB of system memory per training run.

All models were evaluated on the same held-out test set (N = 6,024) which contained equal numbers of images for each race × gender subgroup, ensuring that differences in classification performance were not attributable to differences in the demographic composition of the evaluation data.
We assessed overall classification accuracy as well as subgroup accuracy for racial (Study 1) and gender groups (Study 3).
Classification accuracy was defined as the proportion of test images for which the model's predicted category matched the corresponding human annotation.
In addition to overall accuracy, we calculated race-specific accuracy for Study 1 (White, Black, East Asian, and Indian) and accuracy separately for each race × gender subgroup in Study 3.
Accuracy was first calculated separately for each model and subgroup and subsequently averaged across the five random seeds within each training condition.

To create the test images that varied parametrically in Black-White racial composition, 20 faces of individuals who both appeared and self-identified monoracially as Black (10 male, 10 female) and 20 faces from individuals who both appeared and self-identified monoracially as White (10 male, 10 female) faces were selected from two popular face databases: the Chicago Face Database (59) and the Face Research Lab London Set (60).

text.text: Faces were posed with a neutral expression and direct gaze and cropped.
Next, 760 unique "parent" faces were created by morphing every combination of same-gender White and Black face images (190 each for Black male, White male, Black female, and White female).

Mixed-race morphs were then created from each Black-White combination of parent faces within gender at 10% increments, each producing 11 face images that varied in racial composition from 100% Black to 100% White.
This process produced 190 unique male and 190 unique female spectra, comprising 4180 unique test faces.
Each face morph image appeared on a gray background, cropped, resized, and edited, such that the final image excluded hairstyles, necks, and ears.
Using this test set, we estimated category boundaries along controlled Black-White face-morph spectra for each Study 1 training condition.
Each of the five random-seed models within a condition classified each image along each morph spectrum.
Classification probabilities were then averaged across the five models, and a PSE was estimated for each morph spectrum (33).
text.formatted: Classification probabilities were then averaged across the five models, and a PSE was estimated for each morph spectrum <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(33)</ref>.

text.text: The PSE represents the point along the morph continuum at which the averaged model predictions indicate equal probability of classification as Black or White.
Differences in PSE were assessed using a repeated-measures ANOVA, with training condition as the within-spectrum factor and morph spectrum as the repeated unit.
To estimate conditionlevel PSEs and their uncertainty, morph spectra were resampled with replacement over 1,000 bootstrap iterations.
For each iteration, the average classification curve and corresponding PSE were recalculated.
Mean bootstrap PSEs and percentile-based 95% confidence intervals were then obtained from the resulting distributions.
